job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Sara Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior associate at Kestrel Wealth, a small advisory firm that looks after savings for families and retirees. Each day I prepare client portfolio reviews with the help of an AI assistant, draft the quarterly letters, and sit in on calls with my boss, Margaret, who has run the firm for twenty years. I got a finance degree, top of my year, and I interned at a pension fund and at a local bank. I rent a room with two friends from church, and on Wednesday evenings I run the youth group's small budget. My father is a plumber with his own van, my mother runs a day nursery, and they taught me that you earn your place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's reasonable, and I'd be a little relieved. At work I'd tell Margaret that the tools I use daily are helpful but nothing like a revolution. I'd tell friends to not be pulled into the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel secure. People hand their life savings to someone they trust, and trust comes from years of showing up, which software doesn't do. Margaret's clients ask for her by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, use the assistant to prepare the reviews faster, and spend the time on client calls. I'd work towards my adviser licence this year. I'd put £250 a month into my own investments and keep paying down my loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pleased and steady. I like my work and I'd like it to carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or worry in your own life would stay exactly the same even if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My loan and my parents' van, which is old and might need replacing. Dad is stubborn and won't spend until it breaks. It would be a worry whatever happened with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your week is routine screen work that even a small change could touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot of it. The quarterly letters and the portfolio numbers are screen work, and the assistant already does the first pass. But the client calls and the trust part are human, and those are what Margaret trains me for.

say: I'd tell Margaret the tools are **helpful** but not a revolution.
I'd tell friends not to be pulled into the **hype**.
I'd say trust is built over **years**.
think: I feel **secure**, since clients trust a person over years.
The letters and numbers are **screen work** the assistant already drafts.
My parents' **van** worries me more than software.
do: Use the assistant to prepare reviews faster and spend time on **client calls**.
Work towards my **adviser licence** this year.
Put **£250 a month** into my own investments.
feel: A small **worry** over my parents' old van.
S0.quote: People hand their life savings to someone they trust, and trust comes from years of showing up, which software doesn't do.
fieldNote: Calm is built on **trust** as the product, and she uses the tool daily.
Her family values her answers: **earn your place**.
Small family worries, the van, outrank **AI** concerns.

steps.text: Pass the adviser licence exam this year
Put £250 a month into my own index fund
Use the time saved by the assistant for more client calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's another tool, and the people who learn to use it well will do better. At work I'd propose we use it for the dull preparation so we can spend time with clients. Online I'd share what's worked for me and where it goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm fine but alert. I use the assistant daily, so I know what it does. A bigger firm can replace a junior associate with software, but Margaret's small firm lives on clients who ask for her by name. Still, the entry rung is thinner everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the new tools more on purpose, and I'd ask Margaret to let me take over a few smaller client relationships early. I'd start a small side service helping young couples at church with first budgets and savings. And I'd keep investing for the long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested, with a mild nerve. I like new things when I can see how to use them. It's work for me to stay ahead, but I enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think of a task you did last week. Which part would software take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The portfolio reports and the letters. I spend about two days a month on them and it could be an hour soon. What stays is the conversation with a widow about whether she can afford to keep her house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your manager do differently about hiring people at your level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret would hire a junior less often and want each of us to handle more clients. She'd say it's good for us, and she'd be right in part. But it would mean the next graduate might not get my seat.

I'd propose using it for **dull preparation** so we have time with clients.
I'd share online what's **worked** and where it fails.

do: Ask Margaret to give me a few smaller **client relationships** early.
Start a **budgeting** service for young couples at church.
S1.quote: A bigger firm can replace a junior associate with software, but Margaret's small firm lives on clients who ask for her by name.
fieldNote: She treats change as **work to enjoy**, her adaptable side.

The church budgeting idea shows her community **roots**.

steps.text: Use the new report tools for every quarterly letter
Ask Margaret to hand me five smaller client relationships
Help young couples at church set first budgets
Keep investing £250 a month for the long run

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the pace is the problem, and leaders have to speak plainly about it. At work I'd suggest we talk with clients now about what comes next. At church I'd say we should help each other and not wait for someone to hand out answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd be anxious. If AI can do almost any thinking job better and cheaper, clients might trust the machine too, and the firm might shrink. I use these tools every day, and the better they get, the less the firm needs the person who runs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save £450 a month, aiming for six months of costs, and stop buying things I don't need. I'd also look at what stays human, such as care and community, and think about retraining in financial planning for families, or starting something of my own with my father's trade, a service company for tradespeople's accounts. And I'd ask my parents what the nursery needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, a little sick. But I'd be moving, which helps. I'd pray, I'd work, and I'd keep talking to people I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Say it's the day the announcement is made. What do you tell the people close to you that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents that night. Dad would say a plumber always has work, and he'd be right for a while. Mum would say come and help at the nursery if you need to, and I might.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what happens to the money you owe and the money you've saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop paying extra on the loan and hold cash. I'd also move out of my room to something cheaper, maybe with another friend from church. And I'd have a talk with my boyfriend, Daniel, about whether we marry sooner or wait.

I'd suggest we talk to **clients** now about what comes next.
At church I'd say we should **help each other**.

fieldNote: Even a **power user** sees the paradox of making herself unnecessary.

steps.text: Save £450 a month towards six months of costs
Study financial planning for families at night
Offer accounts help to tradespeople like my father
Talk with Daniel about marrying sooner or waiting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is real time, and companies should use it to train people for jobs that last. I'd say the market will sort a lot of this out if people are free to start things. At church I'd say we should teach the young both skills and character.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel more hopeful than at two years. By 2031 I'd be 27, probably a licensed adviser, maybe with a small practice of my own. Five years is enough time to earn a client's trust the old way, and trust is what machines can't copy quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my licence, move up to client-facing work, and keep using AI to be faster than the firms that don't. I'd start my own small side practice with ten households. I'd save £350 a month, and invest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a seriousness. I'd like to be one of the people who steps up, not waits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about your plan with 5 years instead of 2?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd save and brace. With five I'd build something. I'd treat it like my father treated his van business: start small, do honest work, and let word of mouth do the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you do you think sees this coming, and who doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret sees it, and she's already planning how to be the firm people choose because it has a human face. Most of my friends in finance see it, but they mostly talk about it as luck. My parents think it's overblown.

say: I'd say five years is real time to train people for jobs that **last**.
I'd say the **market** will sort a lot out if people are free to start things.
I'd say we should teach the young **skills and character**.
think: I feel more **hopeful** than at two years.
By 2031 I'd be 27 and maybe have a small **practice**.
Trust is what machines **can't copy** quickly.

Start a small side practice with **ten households**.

steps.text: Get the adviser licence and move into client-facing work
Build a side practice serving ten households
Save £350 a month toward a deposit
Invest £150 a month in a global index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and people should plan in earnest and not panic. I'd say the best thing is to be useful, build real skills and keep your word. At work I'd say let's make Kestrel the firm that does both well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel good about it. By 2036 I'd be 32, married, maybe with a child, and likely running a small advisory practice. I'd worry for those who haven't got my family and my choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd earn my licence and take on more clients, and use AI heavily to be quicker. I'd grow my own client base gradually. I'd also save for a house with Daniel and put money in a pension early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic and grateful. I'd say it's a good time to be young and willing to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what would you start now that you wouldn't with 2 years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather have ten years to build a name and a family than two years of fear, and I'd start with the small honest steps. I'd help a few friends too, so we all go through it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At 32, what do you hope your working life looks like, and what could stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 32 I'd like to have a small firm with a couple of juniors I train myself. What could stop me is a big downturn, a client scandal, or the whole advice business sliding into apps that cost nothing.

I'd say be **useful**, build real skills and keep your word.
I'd say let's make Kestrel do **both** well.

I'd worry for those without my family and **choices**.
It's a good time to be young and **willing**.

Use AI to prepare every review and letter
Save for a house deposit with Daniel
Plan the wedding and a first child around my career

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to build trust or savings. What would help is honesty from employers early, training that leads to real jobs, and a fair market where people can start small businesses without too many rules. And my family and church around me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say people sometimes assume faith and tradition mean I'm afraid of the new. I use the machines every day and I still believe the most valuable thing I can offer a client is that I showed up and kept my word. That's what I'm betting on.

headlineQuote: I use the machines every day and I still believe the most valuable thing I can offer a client is that I showed up and kept my word.
portrait: Sara is a **22-year-old** junior adviser at a small wealth firm, top of her class, who uses AI every day.
She is traditional, values **family, faith and work**, and favours markets and apprenticeships over handouts.
She treats change as **work to enjoy**, and plans around marriage and a practice of her own.
She is calm in mild worlds, **anxious** at two years, and hopeful when there is time.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because there'd be no time to build trust or savings.
whatWouldHelp: Early **honesty** from employers, training that leads to real jobs, and freedom to start small firms.
